passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of four different cognitive training protocols on reaction time in adults aged 18–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group that received no training, Treatment A (visual-spatial training), Treatment B (verbal memory training), and Treatment C (multimodal training). Each group consisted of 30 participants. The mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) were recorded after a 4‑week training period. The results are summarized in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether specific training modalities could significantly reduce RT compared to the control, and to explore variability across modalities.
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time?
explanation: The mean RT for Treatment A is 510 ms, which is lower than the means for Control (550 ms), Treatment B (530 ms), and Treatment C (520 ms).
trap: Picking Treatment C because multimodal training sounds most effective, instead of comparing the four means (Treatment A at 510 ms is lowest).

stem: What type of study design was used in this research?
explanation: Participants were randomly assigned to treatment groups, a hallmark of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Option B may seem plausible because participants were observed, but random assignment distinguishes the study as an RCT.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: Treatment A improved reaction time compared to Control.
options.B: Treatment B had higher variability than Treatment A.
options.C: Control group had a mean RT of 550 ms.
options.D: Treatment C had the lowest mean reaction time.

explanation: Treatment A (510 ms) had the lowest mean reaction time; Treatment C (520 ms) did not. The other statements are supported by Table 1.
trap: Treatment C (multimodal training) sounds like it should be best, but Table 1 shows Treatment A is faster.

stem: What is the standard error of the mean reaction time for Treatment B?
explanation: Correct: B) SE = SD/sqrt(n) = 50/sqrt(30) = 9.1 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 1.7 ms divides the SD by n (30) instead of by the square root of n. C) 16.7 ms divides the SD by 3, which is not sqrt(30). D) 50 ms is the SD itself, which describes spread of individuals rather than the precision of the mean.
trap: Dividing the SD by n (30) instead of sqrt(n), which gives 1.7 ms, or reporting the SD itself as the standard error.
